The project

What would it take to lift the table?

Imagine walking around a coffee table with a camera. Later, you want two things. You want to see the bowl from a position where you never stood. You also want to select a patch of the tabletop in Blender, lift it and save the change. The first task needs a convincing picture. The second needs vertices and triangles that join in the right places.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) stores a scene as many soft, colored shapes. It projects and blends those shapes to draw a picture from a chosen camera. This project changes how a training program decides which shapes to split. It asks whether a smaller collection can draw better pictures on a desktop GPU with 6 GiB of memory, and what kind of editable surface that collection can yield.

At deployment the input is a desired camera pose and lens model. The output is a new RGB image. The scene parameters are already fitted, so moving the virtual camera simply reprojects the same collection of shapes and changes their overlap and directional colors. A point cloud alone leaves gaps between isolated samples. A finite Gaussian footprint can cover nearby pixels, fade smoothly into its neighbors and send a useful derivative back to its center and shape. A triangle mesh makes a different commitment: its faces explicitly specify which vertices belong to a surface.

Notation you will use throughout
Vector, matrix and transpose
A vector such as (x, y, z) collects coordinates. A matrix maps a vector to another vector. A rotation matrix changes orientation while preserving lengths. The transpose, written T as a superscript, exchanges rows and columns. For a rotation its transpose also undoes the rotation.
μ, Σ, σ and Σ with an index
Greek mu is a center. Capital sigma as a matrix is covariance, the spread of a shape in different directions. Lowercase sigma often denotes a scale or a density as defined nearby. A large sigma followed by an index under it means “add these contributions.”
Derivative, gradient and Jacobian
A derivative is the local slope of an output as one input changes. A gradient lists the slopes of a scalar output with respect to several inputs. A Jacobian arranges the slopes of a vector output in a matrix, one row for each output coordinate.
Residual, loss and evaluation metric
A residual is a discrepancy between a prediction and an observation. A loss combines discrepancies into the quantity training tries to reduce. A metric summarizes performance for evaluation. In this project their roles differ: a pixel error can affect training, contribute to a parent’s ranking, or be measured on a reserved view.

Four questions to carry through the guide

  1. Where is a photographed point? Solve its depth from two views, then follow that point through world, camera and pixel coordinates.
  2. What does a Gaussian store? Derive the ellipse it draws, blend it with other footprints and backpropagate a mistaken pixel.
  3. What did this project change? Trace B00 through A05-Abs, calculate a winning parent and replay the measured growth events.
  4. Which experiment supports which claim? Recompute the gradient interaction, derive a mesh zero crossing and explain what the Blender check establishes.

If the matrix notation is new, start each derivation with its numerical example. At the end, use the code walkthrough and eight self-checks to reconstruct the argument without the report.

Inputs

Where were the cameras?

Topics in this chapter
  1. Public photographs
  2. Personal RGB-D capture
  3. Solve one camera pair on paper
  4. Track a point through the coordinate systems
  5. What bundle adjustment actually fits

Find the same corner of the table in two photos. From each camera, imagine drawing a ray through the corner’s pixel. If you know how the cameras were positioned, the rays tell you roughly where the corner lies in 3D. A larger sideways movement between the cameras usually makes depth easier to determine. Two almost identical views give little leverage.

Structure from Motion (SfM) solves for camera positions and sparse points together from many such matches. COLMAP is the software used for this camera model. Its bundle adjustment refines camera poses and points so the projected points land closer to their observed pixels. A pose is a camera’s position and orientation. Its intrinsics describe how the lens maps directions to pixels.

Public photographs

Room, Counter, Kitchen and Bonsai use the supplied Mip-NeRF 360 cameras and sparse points with half-resolution photographs. Garden uses quarter-resolution images. Every eighth sorted image is set aside for evaluating the Gaussian model. Room has 272 fitting photos, 39 evaluation photos and 112,627 starting points.

Personal RGB-D capture

The RealSense D455 recorded color (RGB) and depth (D). Depth was aligned to the color camera. Matching features and fitting camera-axis depth helped establish a local scale. A matte museum segment registered 92 fitting cameras. The Gaussian comparison used 21 selected fitting frames, 90,000 starting points and three reserved depth frames.

How a 3D point lands on a photo

In camera coordinates, a point has sideways position x, vertical position y and forward depth z. Its horizontal pixel coordinate is u = fₓ × x/z + cₓ, where fₓ is focal length in pixels and cₓ is the image center offset. The vertical equation uses y, fᵧ and cᵧ. Doubling depth halves the offset from the center if the sideways position stays fixed. Resizing a photograph therefore requires rescaling its camera intrinsics.

The supplied public camera solution may include feature matches from evaluation photographs. “Held out” here means their RGB pixels were excluded from Gaussian fitting. On the museum segment, the reserved RGB images located evaluation cameras against a fixed local map, and their corresponding depth messages were kept out of the initializer and training.

Matches can drift across similar patterns, reflections and moving people. Only 132 of 317 screened museum intervals passed the whole-route checks. The measured museum results therefore describe that short matte segment. An auxiliary ordinary-video route also stopped when too few frames registered. Better training cannot repair a table corner assigned to the wrong camera ray.

Solve one camera pair on paper

Use a pinhole camera with focal length 800 pixels. Two cameras face straight ahead at the same height. The right camera is 0.10 m to the right of the left one. Measure horizontal pixel positions relative to each image’s principal point. A tabletop corner appears at +40 px on the left and +20 px on the right. What depth would explain both observations?

uL = fX/Z     uR = f(X − b)/Z
uL − uR = fb/Z   ⇒   Z = 800 × 0.10 / 20 = 4 m

Here b is the baseline, the distance between camera centers. Subtracting the two pixel equations eliminates the unknown sideways position X. At a disparity of 19 px the inferred depth would be 4.21 m. At 4 px it would be 20 m, and a one-pixel change to 3 px would move the estimate to 26.67 m. This sensitivity explains how a small reprojection error can accompany a large depth error. In the actual Room pipeline, supplied SfM solves the more general many-camera problem.

Track a point through the coordinate systems

A point on the bowl has world position Xw. Rotating and translating it gives camera coordinates Xc = RcwXw + tcw. The camera’s world position is −RcwTtcw, obtained by setting Xc = 0. Projection divides by camera depth. Conversely, at a known depth z, backprojection gives z K−1[u, v, 1]T, where K stores the focal lengths and principal point. The superscript T transposes rows and columns. The inverse undoes the lens-to-pixel mapping.

Suppose the unnormalized camera ray is (0.75, 0, 1). A sensor reading of 4 m in camera z places the point at (3, 0, 4). Its distance along the ray is 5 m. Confusing those two distances systematically shifts off-center points. The project compares camera-axis depth, uses camera-to-world poses to place rays, and inverts those poses for fusion.

With ordinary photographs, multiplying every scene position and every camera translation by the same positive number leaves the ratios x/z and y/z unchanged. This scale ambiguity is why the public tabletop lift is reported in normalized units. The RGB-D route uses aligned depth on fitting frames to estimate metric scale. After scene normalization, its evaluation explicitly converts predicted depth back to sensor units.

What bundle adjustment actually fits

A track links several image measurements of one putative 3D point. The optimizer projects its current point estimate into each camera, subtracts the observed pixel coordinates and penalizes the residuals. Moving either the camera or the point can reduce the residual, so bundle adjustment estimates them jointly. A robust penalty limits how much one badly matched feature can pull the solution. Holding a reference camera fixed anchors the local coordinate system. On the matte route, fixed intrinsics and confidence-weighted depth factors further constrain the fit.

Features in withheld image tiles gave the local matte map an additional check: median 0.468 pixels of reprojection error and 8.34 mm of 3D separation on those checks. Those numbers describe correspondences in the local mapping stage. The later centimeter-scale mesh discrepancies measure a different output against different observations. One cannot substitute for the other.

Rendering

How does a splat become a pixel?

Topics in this chapter
  1. Build one Gaussian from its stored parameters
  2. From 3D covariance to a 2D ellipse
  3. Rotate the ellipsoid into the line of sight
  4. How the renderer gets the color and opacity at one pixel
  5. Why drawing many splats can be fast
  6. Mix one pixel
  7. A complete forward pass

Think of one splat as a translucent ellipsoid with a soft center-to-edge fade. Its center puts it in the room. Three scales and a rotation let it stretch along the tabletop or narrow along a leg. Its opacity controls how much it can hide. Its color coefficients, called spherical harmonics, let its color vary smoothly with viewing direction, as a shiny bowl’s appearance might.

From a chosen camera, an ellipsoid casts a soft elliptical footprint on the image. The renderer groups footprints into small image tiles and processes overlapping contributors in depth order. For one pixel, the nearest footprint takes a share of the light. The next takes a share of what remains. This front-to-back blending is alpha compositing.

Why call it a Gaussian? How does this relate to NeRF?

Along one axis the footprint strength varies like exp(−½ × (distance/scale)²). It peaks at the center, falls to about 61% one scale away and about 14% two scales away. In 3D, three scales and a rotation define its covariance, which describes the spread and orientation of the ellipsoid. Projecting that spread into the camera gives the ellipse on the image.

A radiance field describes how a scene looks from different positions and directions. The original Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) learns a network that estimates density and color at points sampled along each camera ray. 3DGS stores an explicit set of primitives and projects their footprints. Both combine color contributions along a viewing direction. Explicit primitives let this project count, rank and divide individual shapes.

Build one Gaussian from its stored parameters

Imagine a tiny unit sphere of samples around the origin. Stretch its three axes by positive lengths s₁, s₂, s₃, rotate it with a matrix R, then move its center to μ. A sample y becomes x = μ + RSy, where S is a diagonal matrix with the three scales. Directions of high spread form the long axes of the ellipsoid. The covariance matrix collects those squared spreads and their orientation.

Σ = R diag(s₁², s₂², s₃²) RT
G(x) = exp[−½ (x − μ)T Σ−1 (x − μ)]

Read the exponent as “how far from the center, measured in this shape’s own scale units, squared.” With scales (0.10, 0.02, 0.02) and identity rotation, an offset of 0.10 along the first axis is one scale away and gives G ≈ 0.607. The same physical offset along the second axis is five scales away and gives G ≈ 0.0000037. This is how one primitive can follow a narrow table edge. Its peak response is one. Opacity controls its strength separately, so the renderer uses a unit-height kernel without a probability-density normalization factor.

The trainer stores three unconstrained log-scales, four quaternion entries for rotation, and an opacity logit. Exponentiation makes every scale positive. Normalizing the quaternion produces a valid rotation. The sigmoid function σ(a) = 1/(1 + exp(−a)) converts the logit to an opacity between zero and one. For example, initial opacity 0.1 corresponds to a stored value of ln(0.1/0.9) ≈ −2.197. A change of 0.1 to the logit has a different effect from adding 0.1 directly to opacity.

From 3D covariance to a 2D ellipse

A cloud in front of a camera becomes smaller as it moves away. We can predict the footprint of a whole cloud by asking how a small displacement around its center moves the projected pixel. The matrix of those local rates is the projection Jacobian J. For camera coordinates (x, y, z), each row describes one image coordinate. The negative term in the last column says that moving a point farther away draws its projection toward the principal point.

J = [ fₓ/z, 0, −fₓx/z² ]
[ 0, fᵧ/z, −fᵧy/z² ]
Σcamera = Rcw Σ RcwT
Σimage ≈ J Σcamera JT

On the optical axis, take f = 800 px, z = 4 and sideways scales 0.10 and 0.02 in scene units. The projected one-scale radii are 20 px and 4 px. Doubling depth halves both radii and quarters their footprint area. Away from the optical axis, depth spread also changes the projected location. The Jacobian is a local linear approximation to perspective. Very large splats close to the camera challenge that approximation. The implementation also adds a small diagonal screen-space variance for numerical and sampling stability.

Rotate the ellipsoid into the line of sight

Here the center stays on the optical axis. Its long, vertical and third scales are 0.10, 0.02 and 0.03 scene units. Rotate the long axis toward the camera, then double the depth. Predict which change affects only the horizontal radius.

One-scale radii 20.00 × 4.00 px

This teaching model uses the pinhole Jacobian before the rasterizer’s extra screen-space variance. Its contours are drawn at twice the simulation-pixel scale.

How the renderer gets the color and opacity at one pixel

Let m be the projected center, p a pixel and Q = Σimage−1 the inverse covariance, also called the conic. The effective opacity at that pixel is approximately α(p) = o × exp[−½(p−m)TQ(p−m)]. With center opacity 0.8 and a one-scale offset, the pixel sees about 0.485. A foreground splat can reduce the eventual contribution even further. Keep three numbers separate as you read the code: the primitive’s opacity o, its pixel alpha α, and its compositing weight w.

Color comes from a small directional function. For each red, green and blue channel, fit coefficients of basis functions on a sphere, then evaluate their weighted sum in the viewing direction. The constant coefficient sets the base color. Higher-order spherical harmonics (SH) can represent smooth directional variations such as a visible highlight. Degree L gives (L+1)² coefficients per channel. Degree 3 uses 16 per channel, or 48 per splat. Regular 3DGS appearance can absorb some lighting and pose errors into these coefficients. Recovering material reflectance or relighting the room would require further information.

Why drawing many splats can be fast

A naïve renderer would visit every Gaussian for every pixel. gsplat first projects visible Gaussians, bounds their screen footprints, lists each footprint’s overlapping tiles and orders entries by depth within each tile. Pixels in a tile reuse that list. During compositing, negligible footprint contributions can be skipped and work can stop when little transmittance remains. Packed rendering stores visible camera–Gaussian entries with their IDs. A huge translucent foreground splat can overlap many tiles even in a small model, which is why Gaussian count and render speed have to be measured separately.

For the ordered contributors to a pixel, start with remaining transmittance T₁ = 1. Assign wᵢ = Tᵢ αᵢ and update Tᵢ₊₁ = Tᵢ(1−αᵢ). The weights sum to 1 − Tend because each contribution uses up exactly that much remaining transmittance. Multiply each weight by its contributor’s color and give the background the remaining share. In volume rendering this same logic arises when a ray segment of density σ and length Δ transmits exp(−σΔ) of incoming light. 3DGS uses projected footprint alphas to form its discrete composite.

Mix one pixel

A red splat sits at depth 2 and a blue one at depth 4, in arbitrary units. The blue footprint has opacity 0.50. Move the red footprint’s opacity and watch how much of the blue and the white background can still show through.

Red 60% · Blue 20% · Background 20%
Expected depth 2.50 units

At the starting setting, red takes 60%. Blue takes half of the remaining 40%, or 20%. The background supplies the last 20%. The renderer’s expected depth averages the depths of the contributing splats, weighted by their contributions. Here that gives (0.60 × 2 + 0.20 × 4) ÷ 0.80 = 2.50. A solid mesh at the front depth would give a first hit at 2. This difference matters when turning many such pixels into triangles.

Follow one Gaussian all the way to a new view

Use an 800 px focal length and a principal point at (320, 240). Put a Gaussian center on the camera axis at (0, 0, 4), with horizontal and vertical scales 0.10 and 0.02, peak opacity 0.8 and red-channel color 0.8. For this calculation assume a fully opaque layer at depth 6 with red-channel color 0.2. Use ideal pinhole footprints and ignore screen-space filtering.

  1. Project. The center lands at (320, 240). The one-scale screen radii are 20 px horizontally and 4 px vertically.
  2. Evaluate. Pixel (340, 240) is one horizontal scale from the center. Its front alpha is 0.8 × exp(−½) ≈ 0.4852. Its two layer weights are 0.4852 and 0.5148.
  3. Render. Predicted red is 0.4852 × 0.8 + 0.5148 × 0.2 ≈ 0.4911. Expected depth is 0.4852 × 4 + 0.5148 × 6 ≈ 5.03. Neither layer sits at 5.03. If the observed red is 0.55, the signed prediction error is about −0.0589.
  4. Move the camera. Translate it 0.10 scene units to the right without rotating. The same Gaussian now has camera coordinates (−0.10, 0, 4), so its center projects to (300, 240). The original pixel now lies about two horizontal scales away and receives much less foreground color. The deeper layer shifts less. This change in relative position is parallax, one source of the multi-view information used during fitting.

This chain connects an actual 3D parameter to a visible image error. The next chapter runs the chain backward to decide which parameters to update.

Optimization

How does the room learn its appearance?

Topics in this chapter
  1. The inverse problem inside one fitting step
  2. Backpropagate one mistaken pixel
  3. What changes in memory after backward?
  4. What the matte depth loss contributes
  5. Trace the 7,000 updates
  1. Place the initial splats. Start one at each prepared point, give it the point’s color and choose a size from the spacing of neighboring points. The initial collection only loosely resembles the room.
  2. Render a fitting camera. Compare each predicted pixel to its photograph. The loss combines 80% mean absolute color error with 20% structural dissimilarity, which is sensitive to local patterns. On the matte segment, both models also receive a small confidence-weighted inverse-depth term (weight 0.01). The three evaluation depth frames stay outside fitting.
  3. Update the shapes. A gradient tells the optimizer how sensitive the loss is to a small parameter change. The program differentiates through the renderer. The Adam optimizer uses those gradients and earlier updates to move centers and adjust scales, rotations, colors and opacities. Camera poses stay fixed during Gaussian training.
  4. Refine the collection and repeat. Periodically the program adds splats where finer detail may help and prunes weak ones. Adding splats is called densification. After 7,000 one-camera updates, evaluate images from the reserved camera positions.

The project tests how two strategies handle step four. B00 is the default strategy in the project’s local gsplat trainer. It uses a signed position-gradient threshold of 0.0002, duplicates small eligible splats and randomly splits large ones. It has no count ceiling. A05-Abs is the project’s selected strategy. It changes eligibility, selection and the way each chosen splat divides. Both use the same rendering library, fitting objective, pruning rules and paired starting parameters.

The inverse problem inside one fitting step

During rendering you know the parameters and predict the pixel. During fitting you know the observed pixel and ask how to change those parameters. Several updates could correct the same mistake. A brown bowl that renders too dark might need a brighter color coefficient, more opacity, a larger footprint, a corrected position or a different foreground occluder. Seeing the same bowl from another camera supplies a new constraint. This ambiguity is why visually correct training images alone cannot identify a unique surface.

For the RGB loss, average |prediction − target| over included pixels and channels. Add a structural term based on local means, variances and correlation in image windows. Two patches can have similar average color while one loses the edge of the table. SSIM can detect that change. A fit with mean absolute error 0.04 and SSIM 0.90 has RGB loss 0.8 × 0.04 + 0.2 × 0.10 = 0.052. For the public runs, training minimizes this loss. PSNR and LPIPS are evaluation measurements.

Backpropagate one mistaken pixel

Use a single color channel and one foreground splat above a known composite behind it. Let its color be 0.8, the color behind it 0.2 and its effective alpha 0.5. The rendered channel is 0.5. Suppose the target is 0.65. The absolute error is 0.15 and its derivative with respect to the rendered channel is −1. Increasing this pixel’s brightness would lower the loss.

C = α cfront + (1 − α)cbehind
∂C/∂cfront = α = 0.5   ·   ∂C/∂α = cfront − cbehind = 0.6
∂L/∂cfront = −0.5   ·   ∂L/∂α = −0.6

The symbol ∂ means “vary this quantity a little while holding the others fixed.” The chain rule multiplies sensitivities along the path from parameter to pixel to loss. In one screen dimension with footprint scale s, the center derivative is ∂α/∂m = α(p−m)/s². A pixel to the right and a pixel to the left give opposite signs. In 3D the projection Jacobian carries the signed center derivative back into world coordinates. Color coefficients, rotations, scales and opacity logits each have their own path. An occluded splat receives little color gradient because its T is small. Equal foreground and background colors also make the alpha derivative vanish, even with inaccurate depth.

These derivatives describe a locally fixed contributor order away from thresholds. Culling, depth sorting, pruning and selecting the top parents introduce discrete choices. The trainer alternates differentiable parameter updates with discrete population changes. Absolute gradients supply a statistic for the latter. Parameter updates still use the ordinary signed loss gradient. Replacing Adam’s direction with absolute values would make two opposite corrections point the same way.

What changes in memory after backward?

Adam maintains a moving average of gradients m and of squared gradients v for each parameter. It corrects for their zero initialization and takes a step roughly proportional to −η m̂/(√v̂ + ε). The learning rate η controls the overall step. The shared trainer uses separate rates for centers, rotations, scales, opacity and SH. The base center rate is 0.00016 times scene scale and decays. The base opacity-logit rate is 0.05. These numbers operate on different parameterizations and have different units.

At initialization a point’s scale is the root mean square of its distances to its three nearest other points, multiplied by the configured scale factor. Three neighbor distances of 0.02, 0.03 and 0.04 give √[(0.0004 + 0.0009 + 0.0016)/3] ≈ 0.0311 on each axis. RGB initializes the constant SH term. Higher terms start at zero and the active degree increases every 1,000 updates through degree 3. The initial opacity is 0.1. This provides a coverage estimate in dense and sparse parts of the cloud before the optimizer has seen a fitting image.

One full degree-3 splat has 3 center + 3 scale + 4 quaternion + 1 opacity + 48 color values = 59 floats. At 4 bytes per float, that is 236 bytes. The original Room candidate’s 452,485 splats imply about 101.84 MiB of parameters (divide bytes by 1,048,576). Two dense Adam moment buffers add roughly twice the parameter storage during fitting. Gradients, image tensors, intersections, temporary allocations and allocator behavior explain why training memory needs a separate measurement.

What the matte depth loss contributes

Take a fitting sensor sample at camera-axis depth z and a Gaussian expected depth ẑ at the same image coordinate. The trainer takes |1/ẑ − 1/z|, aggregates valid samples with their confidence weights, divides by total weight, and scales by scene scale. It adds the result with coefficient 0.01. A prediction of 1.1 for a true 1.0 differs by about 0.0909 in inverse depth. A prediction of 4.1 for a true 4.0 differs by only 0.0061. This gives near surfaces greater sensitivity for the same additive depth error. Both matte methods share the term; the public photo runs have no fitting sensor depth.

Trace the 7,000 updates

Read the loop index as zero-based. On an ordinary update, the trainer selects the next recorded camera, rasterizes, builds the loss, backpropagates and steps the optimizers. During the active window it also records refinement statistics. Image attribution reuses that step’s projections before backward; it detaches them so ranking introduces no extra training-loss term. At a scheduled growth event the strategy uses the accumulated statistics after the parameter update.

  1. Index 0 to 599. Learn continuous parameters before the first growth event. The strict start test is greater than 500 and the event interval is 100, so index 500 itself has no growth.
  2. 600, 700, …, 5,900. At each of 54 events, determine growth, then prune, log and clear the window. At index 3,000 the strategy also caps activated opacities at 0.01 and clears their optimizer moments. Later refinement events prune oversized splats as well as low-opacity ones. A reset can temporarily expose contributors that were hidden by opaque ones.
  3. 6,000 to 6,999. Keep the population fixed while optimizing attributes. The replay’s PSNR continued to rise in this part. The extractor reads the explicitly saved final_post_update.pt so its model matches the evaluated state.
The project method

Which splat earns a split?

Topics in this chapter

  2. Give the eligible parents a budget
  3. Rank by what each parent contributed
  4. Split along the longest axis
  5. How the design evolved, one question at a time
  6. Why the absolute value goes inside the sum
  7. Work a complete selection event
  8. Which parent gets one slot?
  9. Derive the budget and inspect an actual training history
  10. Inspect the 54 recorded Room events
  11. Derive the child positions and follow optimizer state

Look for competing pixel corrections

A wide splat might cover both the left and the right edges of a table leg. One pixel wants its center to move left, and another wants it to move right. Signed contributions of +3 and −3 sum to zero. Taking their magnitudes first gives 6, a signal that this one shape is being pulled in conflicting directions. A05-Abs uses gsplat’s existing absolute screen-space position gradients, averaged across projected observations. A splat qualifies when that statistic exceeds 0.0008 and its opacity is at least 0.005.

Give the eligible parents a budget

At each refinement event, the count ceiling rises quickly at first and more slowly near the end. Current headroom equals that event’s ceiling minus the live count, floored at zero. One parent replaced by two children costs one extra slot. If 12 parents qualify with only five slots, the five highest-ranked split. If five qualify with 12 slots, all five split and seven slots stay unused.

Rank by what each parent contributed

Every tenth scoring step, the program records up to four strong contributors to each observed pixel. It credits each with a share of the pixel’s color error and of the target image’s edge strength. A sharp edge can be a paint stripe or a shadow, so it receives less weight. The score combines normalized gradient, error and edge signals. Evidence seen in few scored images receives a discount on the two image terms.

The exact score and schedule

Among eligible parents, divide each channel by its positive median and clip to 20. Image channels first average their accumulated weighted pixel sums over contributing scored observations. With m such observations, support = √min(1, m/3). Rank by normalized gradient + support × (normalized error + 0.25 × normalized edge).

At event k of K, let u = k/K. The event ceiling is floor(initial count + (final cap − initial count) × (2u − u²)), limited to the final cap. Public runs used 700,000 and the matte run used 180,000. The primary protocol had 54 growth events, every 100 loop indices from 600 through 5,900.

Split along the longest axis

Replace each selected ellipsoid with two smaller ones spaced symmetrically along its longest direction. A parent aligned with a table leg leaves two children already positioned along the leg. Both inherit its rotation and color coefficients. Their smaller sizes, reduced opacities and separate centers allow later updates to specialize them. After splitting, the trainer prunes and clears the accumulated evidence for the next event.

One real event. Room began with 112,627 splats. At the first growth event, 21,553 slots were available and 12,642 parents qualified. Splitting all of them and then pruning 1,897 left 123,372. Ranking could only change who received a slot at events where eligible demand exceeded capacity.

Where the method came from. Kerbl and colleagues introduced 3DGS. The gsplat library supplies the renderer and trainer infrastructure. Ye and colleagues’ AbsGS explains the gradient-cancellation problem. Deng and colleagues developed Long-Axis Split. This project integrated those ideas with its event-based budget, contributor scoring, support discount and all-parent split policy, then evaluated the combination against B00.

How the design evolved, one question at a time

B00 → A01. B00 sees a high signed projected-position gradient and either duplicates a small parent (largest scale ≤ 0.01 × scene scale) or replaces a large one with two randomly offset children whose scales are divided by 1.6. A01 asked what happens if only the highest-gradient eligible parents can grow under a scheduled count limit. A count budget controls competition, but a small gradient can hide conflicting pixel requests.

A01 → A02 → A03. A02 added the color error borne by each visible contributor. A03 added contrast in the training photograph. The design hypothesis was that spending a slot where several unresolved pixels share an edge could buy more detail. A textured wall and a silhouette can both trigger this cue. Only a matched experiment can tell whether the ranking helps.

A03 → A04. A04 changed what happens after a parent wins. Two smaller children are placed along its long axis, including when the baseline would have cloned a small parent. This reduces randomness in their initial geometry and lets the two centers cover different regions immediately. Growth per selection remains +1.

Two A05 experiments had different mechanisms. An early residual fallback admitted some parents that missed the usual gradient gate. In an intervention starting from a fixed checkpoint, residual-selected parents lost to an equal count of gradient-selected parents. The final A05-Abs disables that fallback. It changes how the gradient is accumulated before eligibility and raises the threshold from 0.0002 to 0.0008. The budget, attributed image scores and long-axis operator carry forward from A04. These labels describe independent training configurations initialized from the prepared scene.

Why the absolute value goes inside the sum

Consider a simplified white splat on black, centered between two white target pixels at −1 and +1. Its projected scale is 1 pixel and its opacity is 1. Both pixels currently see exp(−½) ≈ 0.607 and want to become brighter. For the sum of their absolute errors, the left pixel gives a center derivative of +0.607 and the right pixel gives −0.607. A tiny move improves one at the expense of the other. The ordinary signed sum of zero correctly describes the loss slope for translating this one center. It conceals the potential value of giving the pixels different centers.

Signed signal in one view = ‖ Σp bp ‖₂
Absolute signal in one view = ‖ Σp |bp| ‖₂

bp is the two-coordinate contribution from pixel p to the projected-center gradient. Take absolute values separately for horizontal and vertical components before adding across pixels. Taking the magnitude of the already-cancelled gradient would still give zero. The symbol ‖·‖₂ means ordinary vector length. For the same backward pass the absolute statistic is at least as large as the signed one. The two training runs will subsequently alter different populations, so that inequality cannot predict their final counts.

The implementation scales the horizontal component by image width/2 and the vertical one by height/2 in these batch-one runs, takes the per-projection norm, then averages over the number of projected observations in the window. That count differs from the image-score count below. A Gaussian can project into the image but never make the top four contributors at any scored pixel. The 0.0008 threshold belongs to this normalized statistic; raw derivatives in the toy example use different units. AbsGS paper

Work a complete selection event

Start with one target pixel. Its predicted and observed RGB differ by (0.10, 0.20, 0.30) in absolute value. Mean error is 0.20. Suppose this pixel’s four-neighbor grayscale Laplacian has magnitude 0.40. A parent with composite weight Tα = 0.30 gets 0.06 units of error mass and 0.12 of edge mass. Other top contributors get their own weighted shares. If the same parent covers 20 pixels of that scored image, all its weighted masses add, while the observation counter advances once. A repeated camera can count again on another scored occurrence.

The Laplacian here is the absolute difference between the sum of four neighbor intensities and four times the center intensity. The image is converted to grayscale by averaging RGB. A constant patch produces zero. The error and edge channels are summed over pixels and divided by contributing observations. That retains an influence of footprint area. A very large erroneous footprint can gather more mass than a tiny one, which helps explain why a score is only a heuristic for future benefit.

N(x) = min(20, x / median of positive eligible x)
h = √min(1, m / 3)
score = N(g) + h × N(E/m) + 0.25 × h × N(B/m)

Here g is the window’s gradient statistic, E the accumulated error mass, B the edge mass and m the scored observation count. Use at least one as the averaging denominator. Invalid or negative channel inputs become zero. A channel with no positive eligible entries contributes zero. The implementation uses the lower middle positive value for an even-sized median. Scaling each channel within the eligible set keeps its numerical units from dominating the others. The support factor discounts only image cues; the gradient uses its own observation history.

Which parent gets one slot?

These five invented parents exercise the project rule. Start with one available slot. Predict the winner, switch off the edge term, then give the event three slots. Each score uses the raw inputs in the table.

ParentgOpacitymE/mB/mScoreDecision
A0.00120.20030.120.082.000Eligible
B0.00160.20010.160.322.488Split
C0.00090.20030.240.042.375Eligible
D0.00080.30040.600.80—At threshold
E0.00200.00430.400.40—Low opacity
Selected for splitting: B.

By hand, A, B and C pass the gate. D lies exactly on the strict gradient threshold, and E falls below the opacity threshold. The three positive medians are 0.0012, 0.16 and 0.08. B has one scored observation, so its support is √(1/3). Its full score is 1.333 + 0.577 × (1 + 0.25 × 4) ≈ 2.488. C scores 0.750 + 1.500 + 0.25 × 0.500 = 2.375. Removing the edge cue lets C win. With three slots both cues can rearrange the ranking while every eligible parent still splits. This is the distinction the 400k Room experiment was designed to test.

Derive the budget and inspect an actual training history

Let the initial population be N₀, the final cap C, and the completed fraction of scheduled events u = k/K. The schedule adds a fraction 2u−u² = 1−(1−u)² of the eventual headroom. Halfway through the events this fraction is 0.75. For an initializer of 100 and cap of 200, the halfway target is 175. With 164 live parents, 11 slots remain. If 20 qualify, 11 split. If six splats are subsequently pruned, the event ends at 169. Pruning frees space for a later event. Unselected parents must qualify again from fresh evidence.

Inspect the 54 recorded Room events

These are measured counts from the original seed-42 A05-Abs Room run. Move to the last event and reconcile the final count with the 700,000 ceiling.

Loop index 600 · ceiling 134,180
Slots 21,553 · eligible 12,642
112,627 live + 12,642 splits − 1,897 pruned = 123,372 live

Derive the child positions and follow optimizer state

Let the parent center be μ, longest scale s and its rotated unit axis v. For split distance d = 0.45, move child centers to μ ± 3dsv. Shrink the longest scale to (1−d)s, and multiply the two perpendicular scales by √(1−d²). Each child retains the parent’s orientation and SH. Its activated opacity is 0.6 times its parent’s. The baseline’s random offsets and the candidate’s symmetric offsets are different ways to initialize the next optimization problem.

For a parent centered at 0 with scales (0.10, 0.04, 0.02), children lie at ±0.135 on the long axis and have scales about (0.055, 0.0357, 0.0179). At the three-scale contour the right child spans [−0.030, 0.300] and the left spans [−0.300, 0.030]. Their outer endpoints match the parent’s ±0.300 and the intervals overlap by 0.060. This preserves the chosen axial extent. The children’s composited opacity and colors can change immediately because their exponents, positions and transmittance changed.

Splitting changes the number of rows in every parameter array. The implementation retains surviving rows, drops selected parent rows and appends two rows for each split. Surviving rows keep their Adam first and second moments. New child moments start at zero, while the optimizer step counter is preserved. The strategy clears interval evidence so the children can earn their own statistics. Mixing old IDs or moments with newly indexed rows would teach the optimizer about the wrong primitive.

Why the earlier pose-probe experiment took a different path

A separate CCD-GS pilot asked whether camera-pose error could make a Gaussian look like a good split candidate. It briefly corrected poses, remeasured the gradient, then compared matched split and no-split continuations. Its utility was the reduction in development RGB mean squared error attributable to splitting. None of the 36 evaluated blocks passed the practical gate. The final report studies A05-Abs with fixed Gaussian-training poses. The CCD-GS pilot supplies a reason to take pose-induced gradients seriously, without supplying an accepted allocation rule. Pose-probe records

The evidence

How much room did the model save?

Topics in this chapter
  1. How to read the measurements
  2. Does it hold across views, seeds and scenes?
  3. Which parts of the method mattered?
  4. Reconstruct the mechanism argument from the controls
  5. Read the quality, resource and repeatability numbers together

For each paired run, the researchers gave B00 and A05-Abs identical initial tensors, the same sequence of fitting cameras and the same held-out RGB targets. A seed controls random choices. Pairing by seed makes it easier to interpret differences between strategies. Equal updates answer what each strategy achieves with the same number of training steps. A separate timed study asks what each achieves before the same deadline.

How to read the measurements

Gaussian count ↓
Each splat carries parameters and optimizer state. Fewer splats generally save storage and training memory. Rendering time also depends on how many footprints overlap each pixel.
PSNR ↑
Peak signal-to-noise ratio summarizes squared color error in decibels. Higher is better. A 3 dB increase for an individual image means its mean squared error is roughly halved.
SSIM ↑ and LPIPS ↓
SSIM compares local image structure. LPIPS compares features from a trained image network to estimate perceptual differences. The arrows point in the favorable direction. The three image scores can disagree.
Original paired endpoints at 7,000 updates, seed 42. PSNR values are rounded. The first four rows use photographic supervision. Both matte runs also use fitting depth.
SceneB00 splatsA05-Abs splatsB00 PSNRA05-Abs PSNR
Room831,326452,48529.99830.737
Counter742,755381,22827.63027.840
Kitchen1,082,362502,53629.91630.212
Bonsai1,020,333463,67830.05530.391
Museum matte485,156179,79228.87228.891

On Room, removing 378,841 splats coincided with a 0.739 dB gain. The saved checkpoint shrank from 187.1 to 101.8 MiB. A timed rendering call rose from 75.4 to 111.0 frames per second on the GTX 1660 SUPER, excluding loading, display and encoding. Across the four indoor scenes, the candidate used 45.57–54.56% fewer splats. LPIPS improved on all four, though Kitchen’s SSIM fell slightly. Matte gained only 0.019 dB and its LPIPS worsened.

Does it hold across views, seeds and scenes?

Bonsai shows why individual views matter. In the saved 8-bit evaluation images, 20 of 37 views improved. Removing the single largest gain changed the mean difference from +0.337 to −0.023 dB. Those saved images are rounded to 8 bits, so this audit differs slightly from the trainer’s full-precision table.

Room repeated across seeds. A controlled replay and two additional seeds gave a mean paired gain of +0.674 dB (sample standard deviation 0.042 dB) and 45.6% fewer splats. All eligible parents fit under the selected 700,000 ceiling at every event in all three runs. Direct cap enforcement therefore cannot explain the Room gain. These three runs used the same previously inspected Room views. They measure repeatability on that scene.

Garden tested a frozen policy. With the method chosen before examining this outdoor result, one seed took B00 to 2,863,759 splats and A05-Abs to 699,712. PSNR rose from 26.032 to 26.397 dB, with 75.6% fewer splats. Here the ceiling restricted selection at all 54 growth events. Garden broadens the appearance test to one outdoor scene in the same dataset family. Its geometry was outside this experiment.

Which parts of the method mattered?

An ablation changes one design choice under controlled conditions. These Room runs help explain the size–quality trade-off. Their replay baseline reached 834,493 splats at 30.125 dB. The selected replay reached 452,409 at 30.757 dB. Keep these endpoints together when comparing the alternatives below.

  • Eligibility. At a 700,000 cap and the 0.0008 threshold, signed gradients left 143,086 splats at 29.668 dB. Absolute gradients allowed more parents through. Lowering the absolute threshold to 0.0002 grew 699,645 splats at 31.084 dB. The selected setting traded some fidelity for a smaller model.
  • Capacity and ranking. At a 400,000 cap, the selected rule produced 399,819 splats at 30.706 dB. Removing error scoring lowered PSNR to 30.688 dB. Removing edge scoring raised it to 30.739 dB while slightly worsening LPIPS. The ranking cues gave mixed benefits when slots were scarce.
  • Split geometry. A04, the earlier signed-gradient budget policy, allowed a separate test of random versus long-axis placement and cloning versus splitting small parents. A direct A05-Abs versus A04 comparison on Room, Counter and Kitchen across two seeds improved PSNR with fewer splats in all six pairs. Five cleared the study’s practical improvement criteria. With all selected parents split in the earlier A04 test, the long-axis operator gained 0.341 dB on average over random splitting across three Room seeds. How those choices interact under absolute gradients is still open.
  • Time. At roughly 90, 180 and 270 seconds of training, A05-Abs led B00 in PSNR at each probe. At 270 seconds it reached 30.236 versus 29.723 dB despite completing fewer updates. Those timings exclude evaluation and depend on the workstation.

Reconstruct the mechanism argument from the controls

Suppose someone asks, “Did the absolute gradient alone give the headline gain?” The original B00 versus A05-Abs pair changes the gradient statistic, threshold, budget, ranking and split policy together. It measures the whole policy. To test a particular mechanism, find two rows that hold the other design choices fixed. The controlled Room replay crosses two gradient definitions with two thresholds under the same long-axis operator, ranking settings and 700,000 cap.

AggregationThresholdFinal countPSNR (dB)
Signed0.0002603,07030.597
Absolute0.0002699,64531.084
Signed0.0008143,08629.668
Absolute0.0008452,40930.757
Single-seed controlled Room study. B00 is the separate replay baseline. The signed rows here already use the budgeted, all-split strategy.

At threshold 0.0002 the absolute-minus-signed difference is 31.084 − 30.597 = +0.487 dB. At 0.0008 it is 30.757 − 29.668 = +1.089 dB. Their difference, +0.602 dB, is an interaction: the effect of switching aggregation depends on the threshold. At either fixed threshold, absolute accumulation actually grows more splats in this study. The smaller headline model emerges when comparing the complete selected policy against B00. Saying “absolute gradients reduce count” loses the condition that made the measured claim true.

The same four rows reveal a design trade-off. Under absolute aggregation the lower threshold buys 0.327 dB at the price of 247,236 extra splats and makes the ceiling bind at all events. At the selected threshold the 700,000 and 1,000,000 caps both admit everyone and finish near 450,000. Tightening the cap to 400,000 saves a further 52,590 compared with the 700k replay, for a loss of 0.051 dB. These are different operating points; the choice depends on the resource constraint and the desired image fidelity.

What the lineage adds. In the archived seed-42 Room pair, A04 reached 30.60068 dB at 597,975 splats and A05-Abs reached 30.73701 dB at 452,485. This comparison changes the aggregation and its threshold together. Across six A04 → A05-Abs scene/seed pairs the prespecified practical gate required at least +0.05 dB, at most 0.001 SSIM loss and at most 0.001 LPIPS increase. Counter seed 43 gained 0.04191 dB, missing the PSNR gate despite a positive change. That distinction separates a favorable direction from the size of benefit the project declared worthwhile.

What the split study isolates. In the earlier three-seed A04 Room experiment, the mean PSNR values were 30.129 (random + clone small), 30.292 (random + split small), 30.425 (long-axis + clone small) and 30.633 (long-axis + split small). Compare the last two to isolate replacing small-parent clones under long-axis placement: +0.208 dB. Compare the two all-split rows to isolate the long-axis operator bundle: +0.341 dB, including its scale and opacity changes. No row independently varies child position while holding its new opacity and scales fixed. All four use signed gradients.

Read the quality, resource and repeatability numbers together

For RGB values in [0,1], PSNR = −10 log₁₀(MSE), where MSE is the average squared difference across pixels and channels. For one image, +0.739 dB corresponds to an MSE ratio of 10−0.739/10 ≈ 0.844. In the report PSNR is averaged over views. Exponentiating a mean paired dB difference therefore gives a geometric mean of per-view MSE ratios. To infer the arithmetic mean pixel error across the scene you would need the underlying errors and weighting. Always inspect the per-view spread as well as the headline.

For the original Room run, count reduction = (831,326 − 452,485)/831,326 ≈ 45.57%. The peak allocated tensor memory went from 1.300 to 0.971 GiB, a smaller percentage change than the parameter count. Image buffers, tile work and other fixed costs help explain the difference. Extraction time went from 8.62 to 8.16 s. The same camera set and fusion grid still need processing. In the historical Bonsai timing the baseline used four loader workers and the candidate used zero. The separately matched Room time probes avoid that worker mismatch.

In the Room repeats, first subtract B00 from A05-Abs within each seed. The three gains were about +0.632, +0.676 and +0.715 dB. Their mean is +0.67449 dB. The reported ±0.04150 is the sample standard deviation of the three paired differences. It describes variation across those runs of Room. The 39 target views are shared across seeds, so treating them as 117 independent scene trials would exaggerate the evidence. Garden adds a different scene with the frozen policy, one pair, one dataset family and a binding cap.

How to defend the improvement. The full configuration fits better average held-out RGB with fewer primitives on the tested public scenes. The controlled Room data support the importance of the gradient definition and threshold. The earlier A04 data support the split operator under signed gradients. Image ranking changes parent selection when slots are scarce, with mixed measured effects. The experiment that would isolate long-axis splitting under the final absolute gradient remains open.
Surface reconstruction

How do soft shapes turn into triangles?

Topics in this chapter
  1. Did the surface get closer to the measured scene?
  2. Compute a surface point from two voxels
  3. Why this extractor, and what its parameters do
  4. Locate the first stage at which depth disagrees
  5. Why the smoothness prior was left out

A splat contains no list of neighbors and has no sharp outer wall. Joining its center to nearby centers could connect the bowl directly to the table. The project instead asks the trained model to predict depth from several known cameras, then combines the predictions into one surface.

  1. Render depth. Load the final post-update model. Render color, accumulated opacity and expected camera-axis depth from up to 64 evenly spaced fitting cameras at one quarter of their training width and height. Keep positive, finite depths with opacity above 0.7. Even for the museum mesh, the extractor fuses model predictions. Sensor depths serve a separate role in fitting and checking.
  2. Fuse the views into a grid. A voxel is a small 3D cell. For each observed cell, compare its camera depth with the predicted surface depth along that line of sight. The sign says which side of the depth lies toward the camera. Clip large distances and combine observations from multiple cameras. This builds a truncated signed distance field (TSDF) where a change of sign marks a candidate surface. The default bounded cube uses up to 192 cells per side and a truncation distance of four voxel widths.
  3. Trace the surface. Marching Cubes looks for sign changes at the corners of each grid cell, interpolates the zero crossing and places triangles there. The program writes PLY and OBJ meshes and checks that the saved vertices and faces load correctly. A thin table leg can vanish if its depth is averaged with the background, filtered out at low opacity or sampled too coarsely.

Did the surface get closer to the measured scene?

The museum check compares three quantities at the same camera pixel. The D455 supplies a reserved sensor reading. The Gaussian model supplies expected depth. A ray cast into the exported mesh supplies the first triangle hit. Depth here is distance along the camera’s forward axis. The comparison uses stable sensor pixels where both methods have a valid prediction for the output pair.

Matte segment, three reserved frames. Median absolute discrepancy is the middle value of the absolute differences from the aligned sensor depth. Smaller is closer. Coverage is the percentage of stable sensor pixels that received a prediction.
PredictionB00 discrepancyA05-Abs discrepancy
Gaussian expected depth7.37 cm7.97 cm
Mesh first hit8.38 cm9.47 cm
Mesh coverage97.30%97.82%

The compact mesh covered slightly more pixels, yet a typical paired depth differed more from the sensor. A gap was already visible before fusion. Repeating extraction at grid sizes 128, 192 and 256 with fixed checkpoints preserved the direction of this gap on pixels shared by all outputs. Grid resolution changed fragmentation. Independent physical accuracy remains unknown because the reference frames came from the same device, with shared calibration and nearby viewpoints.

Topology describes how triangles connect. A connected component is a group joined through shared edges. A boundary edge belongs to only one triangle. Room and Bonsai had fewer components and boundary edges with A05-Abs. Kitchen and matte had more of both. All ten raw meshes had open edges. A Room trial that penalized curvature made predicted depth smoother by its chosen measure, but the candidate mesh’s component count rose from 1,162 to 1,216. The final method omitted that penalty.

Compute a surface point from two voxels

Use D for a rendered depth at a voxel’s projected pixel and z for the voxel’s own camera-axis depth. The projective signed distance is D − z. A voxel in front of the observed surface gives a positive value. Only supported observations in the integrator’s update range contribute. Scale each supported residual by the truncation distance τ and limit its magnitude to one. The field averages those values over views; the following arithmetic uses equal weights for clarity.

Fview = clip((D − z)/τ, −1, +1)
Ffused = Σ(w × Fview) / Σw
Zero-crossing fraction along an edge = F₀ / (F₀ − F₁)

Along one simplified viewing direction, two observations place a surface at 2.00 and 2.04 m. With τ = 0.10 m, a voxel at 1.98 m gets (+0.20, +0.60), averaging +0.40. A second voxel at 2.06 m gets (−0.60, −0.20), averaging −0.40. The field crosses zero halfway along their edge, at 2.02 m. Marching Cubes does this along edges between the eight corners of each grid cell, then connects the interpolated vertices into triangles according to the signs at the corners. This example illustrates the calculation. The public reconstruction uses normalized units.

Projecting and integrating many slightly shifted views can reduce random noise. A depth bias common to all views survives averaging. At an occluding leg, expected depth can sit between the leg and wall; repeated biased predictions can create a bridge in the fused mesh. Increasing resolution samples that biased field more finely. The source of the bias has to be tested upstream as well.

Why this extractor, and what its parameters do

The crop takes the first and 99th percentiles of initializer coordinates per axis, centers a cube on those bounds and sets its side L to 1.2 times the largest span. For scene scale s, default resolution is R = min(192, ceil(L/(0.01s))), voxel width Δ = L/R, and default truncation τ = 4Δ. The rendered depth map is quarter width and quarter height. Increasing R preserves finer zero crossings only where the source depths support them. Doubling R makes eight times as many cells in a dense volume.

Using fitting-camera rendered depth gives both trained models the same extraction procedure. Directly joining Gaussian centers would impose a connectivity assumption. Poisson reconstruction instead expects oriented surface samples, while a Gaussian covariance has no uniquely signed surface normal. Surface-oriented methods such as SuGaR and 2DGS alter the representation or training to favor surfaces. They are relevant alternatives, but the report does not run a head-to-head comparison with them. Curless and Levoy on volumetric fusion

Locate the first stage at which depth disagrees

First evaluate expected depth against a reserved sensor frame. Then cast the same calibrated rays into the mesh. To compare the two models fairly, use pixels where both predictions exist. For example, if one method misses every difficult bowl-rim pixel, its error over its own surviving pixels could look deceptively small. The project reports coverage separately to reveal such differences. A negative signed discrepancy means the predicted surface lies closer to the camera than the sensor reading. Taking absolute values answers how far apart the two are, irrespective of direction.

The matte check accepts finite sensor readings between 0.3 and 6 m. A 3×3 neighborhood must also be valid and have a spread below the larger of 3 cm and 2% of center depth. This filters unstable readings around edges, where an infrared depth sensor can mix foreground and background. It also removes some of the most challenging thin-feature evidence. The three nearby frames share calibration and camera fitting with the acquisition, so agreement here measures local same-device consistency.

The default pairwise mesh comparison above uses pixels shared by those two meshes. The grid experiment uses a stricter intersection shared by both Gaussian predictions and all six mesh predictions. It retains 856,383 of 918,331 stable pixels. On that shared set, median absolute Gaussian discrepancy was 6.94 cm for B00 and 7.64 cm for A05-Abs. For mesh grids 128, 192 and 256, B00 gave 8.25, 8.26 and 8.30 cm; A05-Abs gave 9.31, 9.35 and 9.35 cm. The 192-grid values differ from the pairwise 8.38 and 9.47 cm because the pixels included changed.

Across the three grids, the absolute truncation length in normalized coordinates was held at about 0.1726; only the spatial discretization changed. For A05-Abs, coverage rose from 96.27% to 98.65%, components rose from 695 to 2,284, and boundary edges rose from 9,061 to 36,040. Simultaneously, the largest component’s share of surface area rose from 66.0% to 92.1%. A larger main sheet can coexist with many tiny islands. A single count cannot decide whether a reconstruction got better. The persistent depth gap and changing topology are two distinct observations.

Why the smoothness prior was left out

The experimental prior samples triples of adjacent log-depth values on a strided grid and penalizes the absolute second difference |log zₗ − 2 log zcenter + log zᵣ|. A constant slope in log depth gives zero. Valid high-opacity neighborhoods contribute most when their target colors agree. The color and opacity weights are detached so the model cannot reduce this term simply by changing those weights. At weight 0.01 from update 3,000 the candidate’s curvature proxy fell 3.06%, yet its boundary edges increased from 16,807 to 17,700. This is a concrete case where the optimized proxy improved and the downstream property did not. Surface-loss implementation

Blender verification

Did the edit survive reopening?

On each of the ten raw meshes (five paired scenes × two methods), the project cast a ray at a corresponding target, selected a connected patch and displaced it toward the camera by up to half a voxel. A separate Blender process reopened each saved file and checked the evaluated vertex positions. All ten retained the edit.

The illustrated Room demonstration used a cleaned copy. It removed duplicate or degenerate triangles and tiny fragments, then simplified the mesh by collapsing edges while penalizing changes along boundaries. This took the original candidate from 119,987 to 77,624 triangles. It still had 13,386 open boundary edges. In Blender a shape key stored an alternate set of vertex positions. The script used it to lift the middle of a small connected patch and tapered the lift toward its edges.

A fresh Room replay produced a slightly different triangulation. Its 12-vertex patch also retained the +0.040 lift. The public cameras and points use normalized scene coordinates, so there is no justified conversion of that displacement into centimeters. The reopen test establishes a local, persistent editing operation. A fabrication-ready table would additionally need verified dimensions, closed surfaces and faithful thin supports.

What cleanup changes and what Blender measures

The cleanup stage removes degenerate triangles and duplicate faces (including reversed duplicates). It removes a connected fragment only when it has fewer than eight faces and area below one quarter of the squared voxel width. Requiring both limits helps preserve legitimate small features. Quadric decimation then estimates the surface error associated with candidate edge collapses and reduces the retained triangle count toward 65%, with a boundary penalty of 8. A penalty makes changes to boundaries more expensive; closing every hole would be a separate operation. Normals are recomputed after simplification.

A silhouette check asks whether rays from the same camera still hit the cleaned mesh in the same pixels. In the coffee-table crop, cleanup changed zero hit pixels out of 96,292. In the foliage crop it lost 374 and gained 17. Agreement in a single silhouette can coexist with different depths along the same rays. The thin footstool supports were already incomplete in the raw surface. This comparison separates damage visible before cleanup from changes introduced by simplification.

The raw-mesh test and the cleaned-tabletop test use different selection rules. On each raw mesh, the script finds a corresponding ray hit, walks adjacent faces within a four-voxel neighborhood and displaces a connected patch toward the camera. On cleaned Room, a fixed scene-coordinate seed plus height and upward-normal checks select a tabletop patch. A cosine falloff moves the center most and tapers the offset toward the perimeter. Blender stores this offset in a shape key. A second process opens the saved file, evaluates the shape key at value one and compares measured vertex offsets against the intended direction and peak. This guards against mistaking an unsaved viewport preview for an actual edit.

A radiance field and a mesh can both use the PLY container. Inspect the contents: a Gaussian export stores per-primitive attributes such as scale, orientation, SH and opacity, while an extracted polygon PLY contains mesh vertices and face indices. Editing the mesh shape key changes that Blender asset. The Gaussian checkpoint still renders its learned scene. Re-rendering that checkpoint cannot verify a mesh edit.

Study and implementation

Can you reconstruct the argument yourself?

Topics in this chapter

Trace a single training update in the code, then try the questions below with the answers closed. The derivations and data you need are all on this page.

Read the code in execution order

  1. Find the inputs and initialization. In create_splats_with_optimizers, follow the neighbor-distance calculation into log-scales and the point colors into sh0. Look at the shapes of means (N × 3) and shN (N × 15 × 3 at degree 3). In Runner.train, identify the camera batch, active SH degree, loss, optimizer step and strategy callback. Trainer
  2. Find the forward and backward interfaces. Trace camera matrices, normalized rotation, activated opacity and SH to the rasterizer. The outputs include colors, accumulated alpha and projection metadata. Follow means2d from forward metadata to the ordinary gradient and the optional absgrad collected in backward. Rendering entry point · CUDA backward path
  3. Find both population controllers. Read DefaultStrategy._update_state before _grow_gs so you know the units of grad2d / count. In BudgetStrategy.observe_image, packed contributor IDs are remapped to global primitive IDs. In _grow_gs, follow one candidate through the opacity gate, headroom, normalized score and top-k. The experiment configuration enables the image and split options used by A05-Abs. The class defaults support other configurations. Default strategy · Budget strategy
  4. Find the row replacement. In split, inspect local_offsets, child_scales, the converted child opacity, and the zeroed optimizer rows. Compare the branch that samples Gaussian offsets for B00. Population operations
  5. Find the physical assumptions. Follow the extractor’s camera selection, alpha mask, crop, voxel width and truncation. Then inspect the sensor mask and ray depths in the comparison. Follow the saved Blender shape key into the separate verifier. Extractor · Depth and topology review · Cleaned Room edit and verifier

Rebuild one refinement event from memory

Draw the next fitting camera and render the current splats.
On scored views, attribute detached error and edge masses to contributors.
Backpropagate the fitting loss and take the signed optimizer step.
While refinement is active, accumulate projected gradient norms and counts.
At a refinement event:
  eligible = parents with average gradient > 0.0008 and opacity ≥ 0.005
  slots = max(0, scheduled ceiling − live count)
  split the highest-scoring min(slots, eligible count) eligible parents
  prune weak splats and any oversized splats under the active schedule
  record the counts, then clear the interval statistics
At the reset index, lower high opacities and clear their optimizer moments.

Check your understanding

1. A splat doubles its distance and keeps the same size. What happens to its footprint?

For a small on-axis splat with fixed orientation and focal length, each projected radius halves. Its area falls to roughly one quarter. The ideal center alpha stays at its learned opacity, but it reaches fewer pixels. Screen-space filtering and clipping can affect very small footprints.

2. Can identical RGB pixels encode different depths? Construct an example.

Give two splats the same color as each other and use an opaque rear layer so no background shows. Moving opacity from the rear layer to the front leaves RGB unchanged. With depths 2 and 4 and front alpha 0.75, expected depth is 2.5. At front alpha 0.25 it becomes 3.5. This idealized single-pixel construction proves the ambiguity; more calibrated views impose additional constraints.

3. Why can a zero signed derivative be correct even when splitting would help?

A translation moves every covered pixel’s footprint together. Opposing pixel derivatives can cancel, accurately predicting no first-order gain from translating the single center. Splitting adds a new degree of freedom: each child can move separately. The absolute gate exposes the disagreement, while signed gradients still train the children.

4. A parent has a large color error, high edge score and g = 0.0007. Can it win?

Under the selected A05-Abs rule it fails the strict 0.0008 gradient gate. The ranking only operates on eligible parents. Empty budget slots do not change this rule. The earlier residual-fallback experiment is a different configuration.

5. A live model has 200,000 splats, a target of 201,000 and 1,800 eligible parents. How many remain after 250 prunes?

There are 1,000 slots, so 1,000 parents split. Each replacement adds one net row. The result is 200,000 + 1,000 − 250 = 200,750. The 800 unchosen parents remain unless pruned. Their next opportunity depends on fresh evidence.

6. What control would isolate Long-Axis Split under the final absolute-gradient policy?

Keep absolute gradients, threshold, ranking, cap, all-parent split treatment, camera order, initializer and evaluation fixed. Change random versus long-axis child generation and compare paired seeds. This tests the operator bundle in A05-Abs. To isolate placement itself, independently control child scales and opacities too. The report’s earlier split factorial answers the signed-gradient version.

7. Why can a method cover more sensor pixels and still have worse median error?

Coverage counts where a prediction exists. Median absolute error measures how far valid predictions lie from the reference on the shared subset. An algorithm can fill more holes yet shift surfaces near the camera. Matte shows this: mesh coverage increased 0.52 percentage points while median absolute discrepancy on paired support increased 1.09 cm.

8. A cleaner mesh has fewer components. What would establish dimensional accuracy?

Measure the surface against independent calibrated geometry with known scale, aligned using a documented procedure. Report coverage and error on fixed regions, including difficult edges. Component counts, silhouettes and persistent edits each test a different property. None supplies the missing physical reference in public Room.

Reading the report

Where to find the evidence

The report’s answer depends on the task. For predicting new photographs of the tested public scenes, A05-Abs usually bought better views with fewer splats. For moving a local patch, the saved meshes worked. For measuring the physical table, the experiment leaves the question open. The report reaches each conclusion by comparing images, reopening Blender files or checking sensor depth.

Chapters 1–2 · Question and foundations
Start with the tabletop example, then follow the camera model, Gaussian projection, gradients and depth fusion. The related-work discussion credits the original methods.
Chapter 3 · Implementation
Follow the data from acquisition through training, splitting, extraction and editing. The equations give the ranking rule and the exact child placement.
Chapter 4 · Experiments and limits
Read each table with its scene, split, seed and comparison partner. The paired endpoints, Room controls, Garden transfer, matte depth and Blender operations answer different questions.
Chapter 5 and appendices · Conclusions and reproduction
The conclusion revisits the research questions. The appendices give the Room replay procedure and an evidence register mapping claims to inputs, code and saved records.

How to reproduce the Room example

Prepare the official Room factor-two photographs and COLMAP model, the CUDA-enabled gsplat environment and Blender using the reproduction guide. From the repository root in PowerShell, run the wrapper below with the path to your installed Blender executable. It runs preparation, training with the recorded camera order, extraction, cleanup, editing and independent verification. The fresh rehearsal yielded 119,061 raw triangles, 76,971 cleaned triangles and the 12-vertex edit.

.\report\final_report\reproduce_room.ps1 `
  -Blender 'C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 4.5\blender.exe' `
  -Work 'results/report_room_replay'
